A.explanation: This divides energy $mgs \sin\alpha$ by power $Fv$ instead of work $Fs$, so the units do not give a dimensionless ratio.

B.explanation: This uses $mv$ which has units of momentum, not the gravitational potential energy $mgh$ gained up the slope.

C.explanation: This is $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ divided by $Fs$, the kinetic energy for speed $v$ over work, not the potential energy from vertical height $s\sin\alpha$.

D.explanation: This equals $mgs\sin\alpha$ divided by $Fs$ after cancelling $s$, which is potential gain over work done.

hints: Look at the diagram: $s$ is along the slope at angle $\alpha$, so the vertical height gained is $s\sin\alpha$, not $s$.
Recall the two governing relations: work by force $F$ parallel to displacement is $Fs$ and gravitational gain is $mgh$ with $h = s\sin\alpha$.
Form the ratio $mg s\sin\alpha$ over $Fs$ and cancel $s$ to see why constant velocity $v$ does not appear in the final expression.
walkthrough: Work done by the constant force parallel to the slope is force times distance along the slope: $W = Fs$.
From the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $s$ and angle $\alpha$, the vertical rise is $h = s\sin\alpha$.
Gravitational potential energy gained is $E_p = mgh = mgs\sin\alpha$.
The required ratio is $E_p / W = mgs\sin\alpha / Fs$.
Cancel $s$ top and bottom to get $mg\sin\alpha / F$. This is option D.
